lessons.title: Proximate analysis: moisture, ash, protein, fat, fiber
lessons.body: Proximate analysis is the basic set of tests that tells you what a feed is made of. It measures six things: moisture, ash, crude protein, crude fat, crude fiber, and nitrogen-free extract (NFE). In Africa, you can send samples to labs at universities like Makerere, Nairobi, or Ibadan, or use portable kits. For moisture, weigh a sample, dry it at 105Â°C for 24 hours, and reweigh. If you start with 100 g and end with 88 g, moisture is 12%. High moisture (above 14%) causes mould. Ash is what's left after burning at 550Â°C; it shows mineral content. A feed with 10% ash has a lot of dirt or minerals. Crude protein is measured by the Kjeldahl method: digest with acid, distill, and titrate. If you get 3.2% nitrogen, multiply by 6.25 to get 20% crude protein. That's good for soybean meal but low for fish meal. Crude fat is extracted with ether. A feed with 5% fat gives energy. Crude fiber is the tough part; high fiber (above 18%) means low digestibility for cattle. NFE is calculated by difference: 100% minus moisture, ash, protein, fat, and fiber. For a typical maize grain: 12% moisture, 1.5% ash, 9% protein, 4% fat, 2% fiber, so NFE is 71.5%. This tells you maize is energy-rich. Always test your own ingredients because African feeds vary widely. A farmer in Kenya found his hay had 8% protein, but a lab in Tanzania showed 5% for the same grass species. Proximate analysis is cheap and fast, and it's the first step to balancing a ration.

lessons.title: In vitro and in situ digestibility techniques
lessons.body: Digestibility tells you how much of a feed the animal can actually use. In vitro means 'in glass' â you simulate digestion in a lab. The most common method is the Tilley and Terry two-stage technique. You take 0.5 g of dried, ground feed, put it in a tube with rumen fluid from a slaughtered cow (or a fistulated cow), and incubate at 39Â°C for 48 hours. Then you add acid-pepsin and incubate another 24 hours. What's left is undigested. If you started with 0.5 g and 0.35 g disappeared, dry matter digestibility is 70%. That's good for alfalfa but poor for straw. In situ means 'in place' â you put feed samples in nylon bags (porosity 50 microns) and insert them into the rumen of a live cow through a fistula. You remove bags at 0, 6, 12, 24, 48, and 72 hours. The weight loss over time gives you a degradation curve. For a farmer, you can estimate how fast a feed breaks down. For example, maize silage might have 60% digestibility at 48 hours, while cottonseed hulls only 30%. In Africa, fistulated cows are available at research stations like ILRI in Nairobi or IITA in Ibadan. If you don't have access, you can use the in vitro method with rumen fluid from a local abattoir. Collect fluid within 30 minutes of slaughter, keep it warm (39Â°C), and filter through cheesecloth. Always run a standard feed (e.g., alfalfa hay) alongside your samples to check the method. These techniques help you decide if a cheap feed like brewers' grains is worth buying. If in vitro digestibility is below 50%, it's poor for cattle. Above 65%, it's excellent. Use these numbers to formulate rations that meet energy needs without overfeeding.

lessons.title: Near-infrared reflectance spectroscopy (NIRS) for feed evaluation
lessons.body: NIRS is a fast, non-destructive method that uses light to predict feed composition. You shine near-infrared light (wavelengths 780â2500 nm) onto a ground feed sample. The light absorbed by the sample creates a spectrum, which is like a fingerprint of the feed's chemical bonds. A computer compares this spectrum to a library of known samples and predicts moisture, protein, fat, fiber, and even digestibility. In Africa, NIRS machines are found at big labs like the Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organisation (KALRO) or the University of Pretoria. A single scan takes 2 minutes. You need only 50â100 g of ground sample. For example, a sample of maize stover might be predicted to have 4.5% crude protein and 70% neutral detergent fiber. The accuracy depends on the calibration library. If your feed is unusual (e.g., mango seed kernels), the prediction may be off. Always ask for the standard error of prediction (SEP). If SEP for protein is 0.5%, then the true value is within 0.5% of the predicted value. NIRS is cheaper per sample than wet chemistry (about $5 vs $50) and you can test many samples quickly. But you must calibrate with local feeds. A lab in Tanzania that used European calibrations gave wrong protein values for local grasses. So insist that the lab has African feed calibrations. For a farmer, NIRS is useful for screening many ingredients before sending a few for full analysis. You can also use portable NIRS devices like the NeoSpectra, which cost around $5,000 and can be taken to the farm. However, they are less accurate. Use NIRS as a quick check, but confirm with proximate analysis for critical decisions.

lessons.title: Energy estimation from chemical composition
lessons.body: Energy is the most important nutrient for cattle, but it's not measured directly in a feed analysis. Instead, you estimate it from chemical composition. The most common measures are total digestible nutrients (TDN), digestible energy (DE), metabolizable energy (ME), and net energy (NE). In Africa, you'll often see TDN on feed tags. To calculate TDN from proximate analysis, use the formula: TDN = digestible protein + digestible fiber + digestible NFE + (digestible fat Ã 2.25). The fat is multiplied by 2.25 because it has more energy. But you need digestibility coefficients. For example, for maize grain, digestibility of protein is 80%, fiber 70%, NFE 90%, fat 90%. If maize has 9% protein, 2% fiber, 71.5% NFE, and 4% fat, then TDN = (0.8Ã9) + (0.7Ã2) + (0.9Ã71.5) + (0.9Ã4Ã2.25) = 7.2 + 1.4 + 64.35 + 8.1 = 81.05%. That's high energy. For a low-quality straw with 4% protein, 35% fiber, 45% NFE, and 1% fat, TDN might be only 45%. In practice, you can use equations from NRC (2001) or AFRC. For tropical feeds, the French system (UFL) is common in West Africa. A UFL is the net energy for lactation of 1 kg of standard barley. Maize grain has about 1.2 UFL per kg dry matter. You can also estimate ME from TDN: ME (Mcal/kg) = TDN% Ã 0.04409. So 81% TDN gives 3.57 Mcal/kg. For a 500 kg cow giving 10 L milk, she needs about 20 Mcal ME per day. If your feed has 2.5 Mcal/kg, she needs 8 kg dry matter from that feed. Always adjust for stage of production. Energy estimation helps you avoid overfeeding expensive grains and use cheap by-products wisely.

lessons.title: Anti-nutritional factors and mycotoxin screening
lessons.body: Anti-nutritional factors (ANFs) are natural compounds in feeds that reduce digestion or harm the animal. Common ones in African feeds include tannins in sorghum and acacia leaves, trypsin inhibitors in raw soybeans, gossypol in cottonseed, and phytate in maize bran. Tannins bind proteins and make them unavailable. A feed with more than 5% tannins is poorly digested. You can test tannins with the Folin-Denis method: extract with water, add reagent, and read colour at 725 nm. For trypsin inhibitors, use the casein digestion assay. Raw soybeans have high inhibitors; heating at 120Â°C for 20 minutes destroys them. Gossypol is toxic to cattle; free gossypol should be below 0.02% in the diet. You can test with the aniline method. Mycotoxins are toxins from moulds, especially aflatoxin, fumonisin, and zearalenone. In Africa, aflatoxin is a big problem in groundnuts, maize, and cottonseed. Aflatoxin B1 above 20 ppb in feed is unsafe for dairy cattle. You can screen with ELISA kits (cost about $5 per test) or send to labs like the Kenya Plant Health Inspectorate Service (KEPHIS). For a quick farm test, use a black light: aflatoxin glows greenish-yellow under UV. But this is not quantitative. Always dry feeds to below 12% moisture and store in dry, ventilated areas. If you suspect mycotoxins, add a binder like bentonite or yeast cell wall to the ration. For ANFs, proper processing (soaking, cooking, roasting) reduces them. For example, soak cottonseed meal in water for 24 hours to reduce gossypol. Never feed mouldy silage. Test every new batch of by-products, especially those from oil extraction.

lessons.title: Interpreting feed analysis reports
lessons.body: A feed analysis report can look confusing, but it's just a table of numbers. The first thing to check is the moisture content. If it's above 14%, the feed may spoil. Next, look at crude protein (CP). For a growing steer, you want 12â16% CP. For a dry cow, 8â10% is enough. If the report says 9% CP, that feed is low for milk production. Then check crude fiber (CF). High CF (above 18%) means low energy. For dairy, you want CF below 18% but not too low, or the rumen gets upset. Ash tells you mineral content. If ash is above 10%, there may be dirt or excess minerals. Fat should be 3â5% for energy. If fat is above 8%, it can cause digestive problems. The report may also give neutral detergent fiber (NDF) and acid detergent fiber (ADF). NDF is total fiber; ADF is less digestible fiber. For good intake, NDF should be 30â40% of dry matter. ADF should be 20â30%. If NDF is 50%, the cow will eat less. You also get TDN or ME. For a 400 kg steer gaining 1 kg per day, he needs about 70% TDN. If your feed has 60% TDN, you must supplement with maize. Always compare the report to standard values for that ingredient. For example, cottonseed meal should have 40% CP, 1% fat, 15% fiber. If your report says 30% CP, it's been diluted. Look at the standard error or confidence intervals if given. Also check for anti-nutritional factors like tannins or mycotoxins. If aflatoxin is above 20 ppb, reject the feed. Use the report to calculate how much of each ingredient to mix. If you have maize (9% CP) and soybean meal (44% CP), and you want 14% CP, use Pearson's square: parts maize = 44-14=30, parts soybean = 14-9=5, so 30:5 = 6:1. That means 6 kg maize to 1 kg soybean. Always keep a copy of the report for your records.

quiz.q: What is the first step in proximate analysis?
options: A) Drying the sample to measure moisture
B) Burning the sample to measure ash
quiz.explanation: Moisture is measured first by drying at 105Â°C, and all other results are reported on a dry matter basis.

quiz.q: A feed sample weighs 100 g. After drying, it weighs 88 g. What is the moisture content?
Which method is used to measure crude protein?
quiz.explanation: The Kjeldahl method digests the sample and measures nitrogen, which is multiplied by 6.25 to get crude protein.

quiz.q: If a feed has 3.2% nitrogen, what is its crude protein content?
quiz.explanation: Crude protein = nitrogen Ã 6.25 = 3.2 Ã 6.25 = 20%.

quiz.q: What does high ash content in a feed indicate?
options: C) High mineral or dirt content
quiz.explanation: Ash is the inorganic residue after burning, representing minerals or soil contamination.

quiz.q: In the Tilley and Terry in vitro method, what is the first stage?
quiz.explanation: The first stage is a 48-hour incubation with rumen fluid to simulate rumen digestion.

quiz.q: What does a dry matter digestibility of 70% mean?
options: A) 70% of the feed is water
B) 70% of the feed is digestible
C) 70% of the feed is fiber
D) 70% of the feed is protein
quiz.explanation: Dry matter digestibility is the proportion of feed that disappears during digestion.

quiz.q: In situ digestibility uses nylon bags with what porosity?
quiz.explanation: Nylon bags typically have a pore size of 50 microns to allow microbes in but retain feed particles.

quiz.q: Why is it important to run a standard feed in in vitro digestibility tests?
options: A) To check the method's accuracy
quiz.explanation: A standard feed with known digestibility helps verify that the procedure is working correctly.

quiz.q: What does NIRS stand for?
quiz.explanation: NIRS uses near-infrared light to predict feed composition based on reflectance spectra.

quiz.q: What is a major advantage of NIRS over wet chemistry?
options: B) It is faster and cheaper
D) It works on all feeds without local calibration
quiz.explanation: NIRS is rapid and cost-effective per sample, though it requires proper calibration.

quiz.q: Why is local calibration important for NIRS?
options: A) Because African feeds differ from those in other regions
B) Because NIRS machines only work in Africa
C) Because calibration is not needed
D) Because it reduces the cost
quiz.explanation: NIRS predictions are based on a calibration library, so using local feeds ensures accuracy.

quiz.q: What does TDN stand for?
quiz.explanation: TDN is a measure of the energy value of a feed based on its digestible components.

quiz.q: In the TDN formula, why is digestible fat multiplied by 2.25?
options: A) Because fat has more energy per gram
B) Because fat is harder to digest
C) Because fat is measured in different units
quiz.explanation: Fat provides about 2.25 times more energy than carbohydrates or protein.

quiz.q: If a feed has 80% TDN, what is its approximate metabolizable energy (ME) in Mcal/kg?
Which of these is an anti-nutritional factor?
quiz.explanation: Tannins bind proteins and reduce digestibility.

quiz.q: What is the safe upper limit for aflatoxin B1 in dairy cattle feed?
quiz.explanation: Aflatoxin B1 above 20 ppb is considered unsafe for dairy cattle.

quiz.q: How can you reduce gossypol in cottonseed meal?
options: A) Soak in water for 24 hours
quiz.explanation: Soaking in water helps leach out free gossypol.

quiz.q: Which test can screen for aflatoxin on the farm?
quiz.explanation: Aflatoxin glows greenish-yellow under UV light, though it is not quantitative.

quiz.q: What is the recommended maximum moisture content for safe feed storage?
quiz.explanation: Moisture above 12-14% promotes mould growth and mycotoxin production.

quiz.q: On a feed analysis report, what does crude fiber above 18% indicate?
quiz.explanation: High crude fiber means the feed is fibrous and less digestible for cattle.

quiz.q: What is the ideal crude protein range for a growing steer?
quiz.explanation: Growing steers need 12-16% crude protein for optimal growth.

quiz.q: If a feed report shows NDF of 50%, what does this mean?
options: A) The feed is highly digestible
B) The feed will limit intake
C) The feed is high in protein
D) The feed is high in fat
quiz.explanation: High NDF (above 40%) reduces feed intake because fiber fills the rumen.

quiz.q: Using Pearson's square, if maize has 9% CP and soybean meal has 44% CP, and you want 14% CP, what is the ratio of maize to soybean meal?
quiz.explanation: Parts maize = 44-14=30, parts soybean = 14-9=5, so 30:5 = 6:1.

quiz.q: What does ADF stand for?
quiz.explanation: ADF is the less digestible portion of fiber, measured by acid detergent extraction.

quiz.q: Which of these is a mycotoxin?
quiz.explanation: Aflatoxin is a mycotoxin produced by moulds, especially Aspergillus species.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of adding a binder like bentonite to feed?
quiz.explanation: Binders like bentonite or yeast cell wall can adsorb mycotoxins in the gut.

quiz.q: In NIRS, what does SEP stand for?
quiz.explanation: SEP indicates the accuracy of NIRS predictions; lower values mean better accuracy.

quiz.q: Which feed is likely to have the highest TDN?
quiz.explanation: Maize grain is high in starch and low in fiber, giving high TDN (around 80%).

quiz.q: What is the first thing to check on a feed analysis report?
quiz.explanation: Moisture affects storage and is the basis for other nutrient values.
